Thank you Madam Chair. This report is in response to an inquiry made by Councillor Hill on January 31, 2022.
Regarding the potential risk of expropriation of Wheaton lands currently owned by the city to accommodate the future Saskatoon freeway.
As outlined in the report, the 155 acre parcel owned by the city is located within the RM of Carmen Park and was purchased in 2015 at a cost of $4.2 million or about $27,000 per acre.
The city of Saskatoon has assembled land holdings to accommodate future urban development that now lie in the path of the current alignment of the proposed future Saskatoon freeway.

Although timing and official approval of this project have not yet been determined, the Ministry of Highways and Infrastructure have previously acquired key land requirements on the west side of the river to accommodate the future river crossing.
In early 2019, the province negotiated and purchased 254 acres of private property at a purchase price of approximately $28,000 per acre.
This acquisition would suggest the province is prepared to pay fair market value for lands required for the future highway.

And this is also further supported by conversations with Regina regarding their bypass project experience, as well as conversations with the senior property manager with the Ministry of Highways who has confirmed their policy as to acquire lands required for roadways at fair market value.

Given these circumstances, the administration believes there is minimal risk of ex-appropriation or financial loss to the city, as there would be a willing seller and buyer along with the history of fair market value purchases by the province.

Thank you, good afternoon. My name is Angela Gardner, General Manager, utilities environment.
And I would like to introduce this information report that was prepared in response to Councillor Dubois inquiry on design standards for washrooms in city facilities.

The inquiry also sought clarity on what role the city administration has in mandating design standards for facilities managed by a statutory board or controlled corporation, including the Saskatoon Public Library.
Through the building by law, the city is responsible for administration and enforcement of the national building code and the construction codes act and regulations.
Specifically to this inquiry, the building code outlines the minimum requirements for building design including design standards for washrooms.
The number of washrooms required in a building is dependent on the use of the building and the number of occupants.
The code requires washrooms be provided for each sex assuming the occupant load and the building of the building is equally divided between males and females.
The code, however, does not specify design details such as whether or not urinals are required.
In alignment with the building code, the city has not adopted additional standards related to washroom design and civic buildings above the minimum requirements in the code.

Design decisions are made by our facilities management department, with involvement of professional architects and engineers based on the particular project, giving consideration to program specific user requirements.
This flexibility allows the city to adapt designs that are more inclusive and accessible based on the specific user requirements of the particular facility.
Because there are so many project specific considerations, general additional standards would offer minimum value over the existing practice.
statutory boards and controlled corporations are separate legal entities and the city does not have the authority to mandate them to exceed the minimum code requirements of the by law.
Any changes made to the building by law would apply to all building owners throughout Saskatoon, not just statutory boards and corporations.

Thank you Madam Chair. This report recommends proceeding down the path towards equity investments being included in the city's investment policy through the hiring
of a consultant to provide and develop a strategy and potential portfolio mix to achieve the city's goals.
As stated in the report, the city's current investment policy is restrictive to fixed income investments mainly bonds.
As outlined in the report, the city's portfolio has returned approximately 1.69% over the past 10 years whereby inflation has averaged around 1.95%.
While equities do carry more investment risk, they also offer an opportunity to achieve returns equal to or greater than inflation over the long term,
as well as increase the influence of the city's investments that they can have over other environmental, social and governance priorities.
A properly structured investment policy has historically been able to minimize these risks while achieving positive results for organizations.
Many municipalities including Toronto, Calgary, Edmonton, Medicine Hat, and Moosja have updated their investment policies within the past 10 years
to include equity investments to enhance their return, ESG priorities and address and ensure their purchasing power is maintained.
It is recommended to utilize a consultant to assist the city in evaluating potential portfolio options, evaluate a risk tolerance,
and develop an operating funding strategy to minimize the impacts to the city's operating budget during times of fluctuation in the market.
